title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 9
paragraphs: Having put on French greatcoats and shakos, Petya and Dolokhov rode to the clearing from which Denisov had surveyed the French camp. Emerging from the forest into pitch darkness, they descended into the hollow. At the bottom, Dolokhov told the Cossacks accompanying him to wait there and rode on at a quick trot toward the bridge. Petya, his heart pounding with excitement, rode beside him.
'If we're caught, I won't be taken alive! I have a pistol,' he whispered.
'Don't speak Russian,' said Dolokhov in a hurried whisper, and at that very moment came the challenge from the darkness: 'Who goes there?' and the click of a musket.
('Who goes there?')
The blood rushed to Petya's face and he gripped his pistol.
'Lancers of the Sixth!' Dolokhov replied, neither quickening nor slowing his horse's pace.
('Lancers of the Sixth Regiment.')
The black shape of a sentinel stood on the bridge.
'Password.'
('Password.')
Dolokhov reined in his horse and walked it forward.
'Tell me, is Colonel Gerard here?' he asked.
('Tell me, is Colonel Gerard here?')
'Password,' the sentinel repeated, blocking the way without answering.
'When an officer is making his rounds, sentinels don't ask for the password!' Dolokhov suddenly barked, riding straight at the sentinel. 'I'm asking you if the colonel is here!'
('When an officer is making his rounds, sentinels don't ask for the password. I'm asking you if the colonel is here.')
And without waiting for an answer from the sentinel, who had stepped aside, Dolokhov rode up the slope at a walk.

Noticing the dark outline of a man crossing the road, Dolokhov stopped him and asked where the commander and officers were. The man—a soldier with a sack over his shoulder—stopped, came close to Dolokhov's horse, touched it with his hand, and explained simply and in a friendly way that the commander and officers were up the hill to the right, in the courtyard of the farm (as he called the landowner's house).

Having ridden up the road with French conversation audible around campfires on both sides, Dolokhov turned into the courtyard of the landowner's house. He dismounted and approached a large, blazing campfire around which several men sat talking noisily. Something was boiling in a small cauldron at the fire's edge, and a soldier in a peaked cap and blue overcoat, lit up by the flames, was kneeling beside it stirring the contents with a ramrod.
'Oh, he's a tough one,' said one of the officers sitting in the shadow on the other side of the fire.
'He'll make those fellows get a move on!' said another, laughing.
Both fell silent, peering into the darkness at the sound of Dolokhov's and Petya's footsteps approaching with their horses.
'Good evening, gentlemen!' Dolokhov said loudly and clearly.
('Good evening, gentlemen.')
There was a stir among the officers in the shadows, and one tall, long-necked officer walked around the fire toward Dolokhov.
'Is that you, Clement?' he asked. 'Where the devil—?' But catching his mistake, he broke off and, with a frown, greeted Dolokhov as a stranger, asking what he could do for him.

Dolokhov said that he and his companion were trying to catch up with their regiment and, addressing the group, asked whether anyone knew anything about the Sixth Regiment. No one knew anything. Petya thought the officers were beginning to eye him and Dolokhov with hostility and suspicion. For several seconds, no one spoke.
'If you were hoping for the evening soup, you've come too late,' said a voice from behind the fire, with a suppressed laugh.
Dolokhov replied that they weren't hungry and had to keep moving through the night.

He handed the horses to the soldier stirring the pot and squatted on his heels by the fire next to the long-necked officer, who kept staring at him and again asked what regiment he belonged to. Dolokhov, as if he hadn't heard, didn't answer. Instead, lighting a short French pipe he'd taken from his pocket, he began asking the officer how safe the road ahead was from Cossack attacks.
'Those bandits are everywhere,' replied an officer from behind the fire.

Dolokhov observed that Cossacks were only dangerous to lone stragglers like himself and his companion, 'but surely they wouldn't dare attack large detachments?' he added, as if seeking confirmation. No one responded.
'Well, now he'll leave,' Petya thought every moment as he stood by the fire listening.

But Dolokhov picked up the dropped conversation and began asking direct questions: how many men in the battalion, how many battalions, how many prisoners? Asking about the Russian prisoners in their column, Dolokhov said:

'Terrible nuisance dragging those corpses around! Better to shoot that rabble,' and he burst into such loud, strange laughter that Petya was sure the French would see through their disguise at any second. He involuntarily stepped back from the fire.

No one responded to Dolokhov's laughter. A French officer they couldn't see—lying wrapped in a greatcoat—sat up and whispered something to a companion. Dolokhov stood, called for the soldier holding their horses.
'Will they bring the horses, or won't they?' thought Petya, instinctively moving closer to Dolokhov.
The horses were brought.
'Good evening, gentlemen,' said Dolokhov.

Petya wanted to say 'Good night' but couldn't get the words out. The officers were whispering together. Dolokhov took a long time mounting his horse, which wouldn't stand still, then he rode out of the yard at a walk. Petya rode beside him, longing to look back to see if the French were following but not daring to.

Coming out onto the road, Dolokhov didn't ride back across the open ground but through the village. At one spot he stopped and listened. 'Do you hear?' he asked. Petya recognized the sound of Russian voices and saw the dark shapes of Russian prisoners huddled around their campfires. When they descended to the bridge, Petya and Dolokhov rode past the sentinel, who paced silently and morosely up and down, then dropped into the hollow where the Cossacks were waiting.
'Well then, goodbye. Tell Denisov: at the first shot, at daybreak,' said Dolokhov and was about to ride off, but Petya grabbed his arm.
'Really!' he cried. 'You're such a hero! Oh, how wonderful, how splendid! How I love you!'

'All right, all right!' said Dolokhov. But Petya wouldn't let go, and through the gloom Dolokhov saw him leaning forward, wanting to kiss him. Dolokhov kissed him, laughed, wheeled his horse around, and vanished into the darkness.
